pages.task: Which number on the line squares to `−9`?
pages.why: `3 × 3 = 9` and `−3 × −3 = 9`, and every other number on the line squares to 0 or more. So no number on the line squares to `−9`, and we need a new kind of number.

pages.text:
A quarter turn leaves the arrow from 1 pointing straight up, off the line. No number on the line can do that, so it is a new number, called [[j]]. Times `j` turns an arrow 90° anticlockwise, and two quarter turns make a half turn, so `j × j = −1`. Mathematicians write `i` for the same number; engineers write `j`, because `i` already means current.
Three quarter turns, 270°, done twice make 540° and land on `−1` too. That arrow points straight down, which is `j` turned half round, `−1 × j`: it is `−j`.

pages.text:
People call `j` [[the square root of −1]], and in the same way read `√−9` as `j3`, since `(j3)² = −9`. People differ on which comes first. Some start from `j = √−1` and get `j × j = −1` from it; others call that start unjustifiable, as it leads to misconceptions. This lesson leads with `j × j = −1`.
Here is one muddle. Read `√−4` as `j2`. The usual rule `√a × √b = √(ab)` gives `√36 = 6`, but `j2 × j3 = j × j × 6 = −6`: two quarter turns and a stretch to 6. When both numbers under the roots are negative, write each with `j` first.

pages.text:
Back to `x² + 2x + 5 = 0`. Here `a = 1`, `b = 2` and `c = 5`, so `b² − 4ac = 4 − 20 = −16`. That is `(j4)²`, so the formula gives `x = (−2 ± j4) ÷ 2 = −1 ± j2`, the ÷ 2 being `2a`.
An ordinary number plus a `j` part is a [[complex number]], in general `a + jb` (new letters, not the quadratic's). Here `−1` is its [[real part]] and 2 its `j` part, also called the [[imaginary part]]. That is only a name: later lessons measure the `j` part of a circuit in ohms.
